expected.title: Legazpi's Expedition
expected.lessonRecap: Legazpi left Mexico in 1564; the expedition reached the islands and established a Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565. Legazpi commanded; Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge. A sponsor’s aim is different from a task or result. Local opposition, force and an agreement involving Tupas all belong in Cebu’s history; one action is not everyone’s opinion. A maintained Spanish base differs from a visit, but one settlement does not prove effective control everywhere. San Pedro returned from Cebu to Mexico in 1565. Salcedo captained, Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge and the crew carried out the voyage.

A return connection could carry news, people and supplies across the Pacific. In 1565, San Pedro sailed from Cebu to Mexico. Felipe de Salcedo captained the ship; Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge, with other navigators and crew.

expected.decisionSituation: What evidence would help check the reach of an order issued from a colonial base?
expected.content:
Manila became a colonial governing center. Legazpi established a city council there in 1571. A council is a group with governing responsibilities; an institution is an organized body with continuing duties.

Try a fictional council record: an order was issued. Ask where it was carried out, who supplied resources and how communities responded. Issuing an order and enforcing it everywhere are different claims.

expected.content:
Acting beyond a base required messages, supplies, people and relationships. A threat or use of force can change the circumstances of a response; an official’s favorable label is not enough. Negotiation, adaptation and resistance describe actions in a setting, not permanent labels for whole peoples. Issuing an order is different from enforcing it. Terrain, supplies, local organization and resistance all mattered. Ifugao resistance and later Sulu diplomacy question universal-control claims in different settings and periods.
